newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban chief says executed president deserved fate.
newsitem.headline: Taleban chief says executed president deserved fate.

text.p: The Taleban militia's top leader in Kabul, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, said on Friday that executed former President Najibullah deserved his fate.

"He killed so many Islamic people and was against Islam and his crimes were so obvious that it had to happen. He was a communist," Rabbani told a news conference in the presidential palace in the centre of Kabul, which the Taleban captured early on Friday.

The Taleban appeared in full control of Kabul, announcing it was setting up an Islamic state and executing former President Najibullah as one of its first acts. Afghan government troops had abandoned the city hours before the Taleban entered.
The bodies of Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were strung up from a concrete post at the gates of the presidential palace as thousands crowded around to watch.
Eyewitnesses said the city of 1.5 million was calm and streets were bustling with pedestrians, cyclists and cars, and shops and markets were open despite an Islamic holiday.
The militia's tanks had pulled back to the sidestreets but militiamen were reported driving around in trucks waving the white flag of the Taleban.

Rabbani said government leaders who fled Kabul before the takeover would be judged according to Islam if they were caught, a reference to President Burhanuddin Rabbani, Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
He said the men were believed to have fled to Jabal us-Sharaj, the headquarters of military chief Masood at the entrance to the Panjshir valley, or to the valley itself.
"Our enemies have escaped. We have taken Bagram (airbase) but they have gone beyond Bagram. I have no details but maybe they are in Jabal us-Sharaj or the Panjshir," he said.
The airbase is about 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.
"The message is very clear. Anyone who works against Islam will meet the same fate. Anyone who serves Islam can live peacefully," he said.

Afghanistan's ambassador to India said that President Rabbani and other members of his government were about 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul. He said the government still controlled 13 of Afghanistan's 31 provinces.
The Taleban's Rabbani, no relation to the president, has been appointed head of an interim six-man ruling council set to govern Afghanistan until a new administration can be decided.
The bearded 38-year-old religious scholar turned fighter said a strict Islamic system would be imposed throughout the country, including Islamic punishments such as amputating the hands of thieves.
He said male government employees were welcome to return to their duties.
"For women we will decide according to Islamic principles where and how they can work."
He said the Taleban were not opposed to women's education but it had to be within the framework of Islam.
Rabbani also said the Taleban had no quarrel with northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum because he had renounced his communist past and was now acting as a Moslem.
Dostum controls northern Afghan provinces with links to the neighbouring Central Asian states.
"He has shown himself to be a good Moslem. We have good honest relations with him. We are cooperrating and we hope there will be no problems between us."

Asked if there would be a role in the new Islamic government for former Afghan King Zahir Shah, Rabbani said: "Time and again we have said that every Afghan Moslem can serve his nation. Zahir Shah can also come and serve his nation."
